segments.t: Art director Vika Goncharova steps into the chef's office to thank the new head chef, German Land. He recently took the blame for a prank and saved Vika from being fired by Dmitry Nagiyev. Let's listen to their polite exchange in Russian.
Let's go through Vika and German's conversation in the office line by line.
'Viktoriya Sergeyevna, come in, please.' German uses a polite everyday Russian courtesy expression that sets the tone of the conversation right away.
'I wanted to thank you once again.' In everyday Russian, 'wanted' flows straight into 'to thank' without extra linking words.
'I want to say a big thank you to you.' Vika uses a polite everyday Russian courtesy expression that sets the tone of the conversation right away.
'You saved me from being fired.' Notice how Russian puts 'to save, to rescue' and 'dismissal, resignation, firing' together in a short, direct phrase where word endings show how the ideas connect.
'I do not know how to thank you.' Putting the short word for 'not' right in front of the action word is all Russian needs to make a sentence negative, with no extra helper words like 'do' or 'did'.
'Perhaps you will try this dessert?' German offers a culinary treat using a modal phrase meaning perhaps and a polite second-person plural verb.
'Did you prepare it yourself just now?' An emphatic plural pronoun highlights that the head chef made the dish personally.

'There is no need for any special gratitude.' Putting the short word for 'not' right in front of the action word is all Russian needs to make a sentence negative, with no extra helper words like 'do' or 'did'.
'After all, you and I are friends.' Russian expresses 'you and I' naturally with a first-person plural inclusive phrase, softened by a conversational particle.
'Well, at least in the future.' Spoken Russian keeps this brief and expressive, built right around 'prospect, future; perspective' without extra helper words.
'I wish you bon appetit.' German pairs 'wish' with 'appetite' directly, since spoken Russian skips English filler words like 'the', 'a', and 'is'.
'This looks simply delicious.' Vika compliments the presentation using a third-person singular verb and an adverb of taste. Now let's hear their office exchange again from beginning to end.

German charms Vika with a delicate dessert and hints that he hopes they will become more than colleagues. Notice the formal plural pronouns they use to maintain professional distance. See you next time!
